extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of humor, theorists and critics analyzing joking and amusement
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Noël Carroll's six jointly necessary conditions to evaluate whether a subject is in a state of comic amusement toward an object, and to analyze why a joke succeeds or fails for an audience. Useful for theoretical analysis of humor, audience studies, and critique of specific jokes or performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object is a perceived incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: S regards O as incongruous — as departing from some norm, expectation, schema, or pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perception of an incongruity is the basic cognitive condition for amusement; without (1) 'there is nothing to be amused at — only mere experience.' The incongruity must be perceptible to the subject (not merely alleged by an analyst).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-threatening
rubrics_metrics.description: S regards O as not threatening to S's safety, well-being, or interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the object is felt as a real threat, fear or anxiety crowds out amusement and the reaction will be fear rather than laughter. The subject must judge the incongruity as harmless in a way relevant to their safety/interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not anxiety-producing
rubrics_metrics.description: S is not anxious about O; anxiety in any form (social, moral, existential) blocks comic amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond physical threat, any form of anxiety directed at the incongruity prevents amusement. If the incongruity produces worrying or existential concern, the mental state will be distinct from comic amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not annoying / not vexing
rubrics_metrics.description: S does not find O irritating, frustrating, or distasteful in a way that produces negative affect competing with amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the incongruity produces irritation or vexation, that negative affect competes with and defeats amusement — the incongruity becomes irritating rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: No genuine problem-solving attitude is enlisted
rubrics_metrics.description: S is not engaged in trying to seriously resolve, fix, or address the incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject must play with the incongruity rather than adopt a serious problem-solving stance; if one is trying to resolve the mismatch, the mental attitude is not amusement but a practical or analytic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoyment is taken in the pertinent incongruity, with experience of levity
rubrics_metrics.description: S enjoys the incongruity itself — and the enjoyment has the phenomenal quality of levity (lightness, buoyancy), not weighty insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure must be focused on the incongruity and experienced as levity. Without (6) the cognitive shift may produce admiration, awe, or insight rather than amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pertinent incongruity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The incongruity must be pertinent — concerning features central to one's understanding of the object — and must be held as the focus of enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every oddity counts; the incongruity must concern central features (not arbitrary peripheral oddities) and the subject must take pleasure in that very mismatch. This rules out cases where the supposed incongruity is irrelevant to what actually amuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-construction / shared-norm dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic amusement plays a constructive social role: laughter affirms shared norms, builds cohesion, and demarcates communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful joke depends on shared background norms and aesthetic sensibility. By laughing together audiences affirm shared expectations, create group cohesion, and mark who belongs—so recognition of the incongruity is community-relative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate comic moralism (humor and ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral defects in a joke can reduce its funniness when the violated moral is strongly held, but moral defects do not always reduce funniness; context, audience, and performance can buffer them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ethical valence of content interacts with amusement: if the audience strongly endorses the violated norm, funniness may be reduced. Audience composition matters—jokes that work in-group can fail out-group because the violated norm matters more outside the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist (questions for identifying comic amusement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of practical questions to determine whether Comic Amusement is present for a subject/audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions diagnostically: Is there a perceivable incongruity? Is the audience free of threat, anxiety, vexation, and serious problem-solving toward it? Is the enjoyment focused on the pertinent incongruity? Does the experience have the quality of levity? Is the relevant background norm shared by the audience?
